pr_title: kubelet/client: collapse transport wiring onto standard approach
pr_body:
Signed-off-by: Monis Khan <mok@microsoft.com>

/kind bug

Fixes #114588

```release-note
The Kubernetes API server now correctly detects and closes existing TLS connections when its client certificate file for kubelet authentication has been rotated.
```
pr_comments:
/assign @aojea @liggitt 
(because I know how much you both love client-go TLS hacks)

Here is my understanding of the issue:

- client-go will automatically reload client certs if they are purely file based
- but it only does the connection closing logic if you go through the `tlsTransportCache.get` method because that is reliant on the dialer `=>` i.e. connection closing is about the `http.Transport` and not the `tls.Config`
- in the `KAS -> kubelet` backend call, for `pods/exec` we always create new connections because it is our custom upgrade path code `=>` so the client cert file is both being reloaded and new connections are being spun up
- in the `KAS -> kubelet` backend call, for `pods/log` we use a shared `http.Transport` which will re-use connections / always has the same `tls.Config` `=>` so even though the client cert file is being reloaded, connections are never closed
- the kubelet `request.Authenticator` does request level checks for client cert authn, on the re-used `log` connection it will see a client cert that is no longer valid (because it has since expired)

> * in the `KAS -> kubelet` backend call, for `pods/exec` we always create new connections because it is our custom upgrade path code `=>` so the client cert file is both being reloaded and new connections are being spun up

issue_context.title: kube-apiserver doesn't reload the kubelet client certificate/key on each logs query
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

We bootstrap our clusters with kubeadm (through clusterapi), but provide our own end certs to shorten the certificate validity period.

Because of the shortened validity period, we rotate the file-based endcerts frequently. Recently we started noticing that after performing a certificate rotation, usage of `kubectl logs` was failing with

```sh
error: You must be logged in to the server (the server has asked for the client to provide credentials)
```

From there, we looked at the kube-apiserver and kubelet logs and found log lines like the following:

```
"Unable to authenticate the request due to an error" err="verifying certificate SN=<REMOVED>, SKID=<REMOVED>, AKID=<REMOVED> failed: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2022-12-17T02:31:09Z is after 2022-12-17T00:16:30Z"
```

So it looks like kube-apiserver didn't reload the new kubelet client certificate. This issue typically goes away if we restart the kube-apiserver container or continue to run `kubectl logs` in a loop.


### What did you expect to happen?

Being able to replace/rotate the kube-apiserver kubelet client certificate/key without causing failure for any logs or node proxy commands/operations.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We were able to get a repro outside of our environment with the following steps.

1. Created a cluster-api cluster on azure with CAPZ using the standard quickstart flow plus some minor tweaks:
- Added ` kubelet-certificate-authority: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt` as an apiserver argument.
- Added ` rotate-server-certificates: "true"` as a kubelet argument.
- Used kubernetes version 1.23.6 and 1.23.15
2. Manually approved the kubelet server certificate csrs using `kubectl certificate approve`
3. In one shell continually ran `kubectl logs` and `kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<NODE_NAME>/proxy/logs`
4. ssh'd into the controlplane node in another shell. ran  `mv /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt.bak` and vice-versa.

From these steps I was able to see `kubectl logs` commands be successful when there was no certificate file and failed when the certificate file was present. Eventually, the kube-apiserver picks up the up-to-date certificate/file.

I don't know the internals here, but it seems like kube-apiserver was using some sort of cached-connection which had the stale certificate.

### Anything else we need to know?

We believe this used to work in kubernetes v1.21 and below. Need to confirm this by spinning up downlevel clusters.

Thanks. I don't believe this is a kubectl related issue but I can get another repro with the correct kubectl version.

Did some printf debugging in kube-apiserver. This issue doesn't look like it's a problem with reloading the new kubelet client certificate/key. It actually looks due to existing kube-apiserver => kubelet server connections. 

Verifying with netstat, it looks like during a client certificate reload, kube-apiserver is not closing existing client connections.

I don't have a strong familiarity with the code but I wonder if it would be possible to use [dynamicClientCert](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/transport/cert_rotation.go#L42) with the kubelet_client. It looks like the dynamicClientCert closes connections when it detects a certificate rotation.

Looks like the kubelet_client code ends up using [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/b69cda3e4e09e1b956d42709fbadf12e6c0f24b7/transport/transport.go#L323) certificate loading callback today. (which doesn't close existing connections.)
Also I still haven't been able to trace when this issue first started. Does anyone know if there were some changes in the kube-apiserver => kubelet connections to make them cached/longer-lived?

I have this sample commit that seems to fix the issue. https://github.com/zawachte/kubernetes/commit/b4882c7601c27ed5ce562ecf6c2512fdb1496169

This follows the pattern that client-go uses for client certificate reload. If any of the maintainers think this is the correct approach, I can clean up the commit and add tests.
